lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Respond to an imagined painting of a crowded train in warm oranges. Write describe, respond and connect sentences.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Describe: crowded carriages in orange light. Respond: busy and tense because warm colours are packed tightly. Connect: like my peak-hour bus.' Structure is complete and polite.

WATCH FOR
Only saying 'I like it' or 'I hate it'. A Year 4 response needs reasons from the artwork.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Write a full response (describe, respond, connect) to a painting you choose. Share with a family member and note one different opinion they had and the evidence they used.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Example: Cleo writes, 'I see layered cool blues with one warm window light. It feels hopeful because the light is the brightest spot. It reminds me of waiting for family to come home. Someone else might feel lonely instead, and that is also fair.'

TRY FIRST
Respond to an imagined painting of a crowded train in warm oranges. Write describe, respond and connect sentences.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Describe: crowded carriages in orange light. Respond: busy and tense because warm colours are packed tightly. Connect: like my peak-hour bus.' Structure is complete and polite.
teach_steps.explain:
A written or spoken response to a painting uses describe → respond → connect. Describe the subject and elements, respond with feeling or idea plus reason, then connect to your own experience or another artwork without claiming your view is the only right one. Use respectful language about artists and other viewers.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the elements, techniques or performance choices that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. For movement or instruments, use a clear space, ask an adult to be nearby and stop if anything feels unsafe. You may always describe a choice instead of performing it. One deliberate artistic choice with a named effect is more useful than a longer praise sentence.
teach_steps.notice: Only saying 'I like it' or 'I hate it'. A Year 4 response needs reasons from the artwork. Name the element or technique and its effect, not just decoration.
